arxiv:2611.22055.text: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers. From Hyunjong Ok and colleagues. When a language model writes a network's weights by hand, should it still use a Transformer? In tests with ten examples and little guidance, three language models often designed a sparse table of facts instead. These models reached up to 54.4 percent accuracy and outperformed the most accurate Transformer written by the same model, using about 1,800 times fewer parameters. The results suggest that tables can be easier to write and repair, and may run faster on graphics processors.

arxiv:2611.22275.text: Heave-Ho: Decentralized Long-Horizon Multi-Humanoid Collaboration. From Ting-Hsuan Chen and colleagues. Coordinating humanoid robots over long tasks is difficult because they must move together, handle objects, and stay in sync. Heave-Ho combines decentralized control based on each robot's local observations with a vision-language planner and spoken leader-follower coordination. Trained with two robots, it scales to teams of up to ten and works with different robot types without retraining. Tests show it outperforms baseline methods, and real-world trials demonstrate robust collaboration.

arxiv:2611.23143.text: TCP4D: A Unified Tool-Center-Point Tracking and Generation Model for Robot Manipulation. From Haosong Peng and colleagues. Recovering robot movements and gripper states from ordinary video is difficult, especially when applying demonstrations to different robots. TCP4D uses a shared four-dimensional scene model to track a robot's tool position and predict future movements from video, robot observations, and language instructions. It also turns existing videos into demonstrations for other robot designs without needing the original robot's recorded movements. The model tracks motion accurately, works with just ten demonstrations for a new robot, and improves target-robot success when original and converted demonstrations are trained together.

arxiv:2611.22115.text: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks. From Xingchen AGI Lab and colleagues. Training frontier language models on domestic chips requires balancing model size, computing cost, and long-running workloads. Xing 4 combines studies of model design with training infrastructure built for Ascend chips, including methods to manage distributed computing, memory, and host processor use. The system supported pretraining a two-hundred-eighty-five-billion-parameter model on eight thousand one hundred ninety-two Ascend 910C cards. For agent training, the team also built TeleGym, which links task execution, evaluation, and model improvement while handling tasks that take different amounts of time.

arxiv:2611.23226.text: FastFrames: Video Generation at Interactive Latency. From Gene Chou and colleagues. Autoregressive video models can respond to new inputs, but they have been too slow for fluid interaction. FastFrames speeds them up by replacing parts of the inference process, including video decoding and cache updates, with lighter alternatives. On a single B200 graphics processor, its smaller model generates a frame in thirty-six milliseconds while matching the quality of a model that is nearly eight times slower. A larger version delivers higher visual quality and realism, enabling real-time video generation guided by cameras or physics.

arxiv:2611.23144.text: pi to the 4: A Foundation Model for 4D Scene Geometry and Motion. From Yifan Wang and colleagues. Turning uncalibrated images and videos into a consistent account of scene shape, camera movement, and object motion is a challenging problem. The model estimates dense geometry, camera poses, and real-world scale, while also tracking points and identifying moving objects across multiple views. It ranks best on average in geometry tests and performs competitively on tracking and segmentation, with about half a billion parameters. It can reconstruct scenes from thousands of images in one pass, despite training on at most sixty-four views at a time.

arxiv:2611.23219.text: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve? From Shobhita Sundaram and colleagues. Can language model agents devise their own learning methods, or must people tell them how to improve? In a gameplay test, a frozen model received a compute budget and tools to gather experience and edit text documents, then experimented without a prescribed learning loop or real-world data. Capable models improved by using strategies resembling established ideas about self-directed learning and self-generated curricula. Their written learning materials also helped on outside tasks with different game lengths, mechanics, and three-dimensional navigation.

arxiv:2611.22565.text: MillBill: A Machining Agent with Geometric Feedback. From Gennadii Savrasov and colleagues. Turning a computer-aided design model into a machining program requires both process knowledge and precise geometry. MillBill separates the decisions about machining from the geometric work, using a language model to propose operations and cutting settings, then a simulator to build toolpaths, check material removal, and guide revisions. It also plans setups around which surfaces the cutters can physically reach. On the evaluated tasks, MillBill with Qwen3.8-27B outperformed frontier models that built their own geometry and toolpath workflows.

arxiv:2611.23108.text: FMT: Lossless Image Compression in a Fixed Number of Parallel Steps. From Ammar Ali. Learned lossless image codecs can make smaller files, but they often take seconds to decode, which limits their use in image archives and training. FMT is a format that organizes image values into a coarse-to-fine tree, letting a graphics processor predict and decode each step in parallel. Its decoding takes a fixed number of sequential steps, regardless of image size. On the same graphics processor, FMT decoded Kodak photos nine to sixty-one times faster than tested learned codecs, at the same or smaller file size.

arxiv:2611.22563.text: CADMAGEDDON: High-Fidelity CAD Reconstruction with Local Inference. From Oleg Pavlov and colleagues. Reconstructing editable computer-aided design models from meshes can expose proprietary parts to external services, while local systems can be costly to run. CADMAGEDDON is an open-source agent designed to work on a single graphics card or a current-generation laptop. It breaks reconstruction into simple visual decisions and uses geometric tools for precise construction. With a mid-sized model, it outperforms earlier approaches, including systems using frontier models, on all main reconstruction benchmarks, and connects with FreeCAD workflows.

arxiv:2611.23034.text: M3OPD-Reasoner: An Open Recipe for Post-Training Multimodal Reasoning with Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. From Nguyen Quang Trung and colleagues. Training one vision-language model to reason across images and video can make it harder to capture skills from different domains. M3OPD-Reasoner trains separate domain experts, then teaches one student from their responses, and further trains that student on mixed data. Across twenty-one benchmarks, the student closely matched each expert in its own domain and outperformed mixed-training baselines on the same prompts. Adding mixed-data training improved it further without collapse, showing the two stages can build on each other.

arxiv:2611.21791.text: Regularized Score Centering. From Hao Bai and colleagues. Asynchronous reinforcement learning can become unstable when training uses data from older policies or differs from inference. Score centering reduces extreme gradients, but can still fail when the learner drifts far from the policy that produced the data. Regularized Score Centering adds a penalty that keeps the learner's next-token choices close to that earlier policy, and analysis shows this improves convergence guarantees. Across six agentic tasks, it improves sample efficiency and reaches top performance, including a fourteen point three percent gain on AppWorld and nine point nine times the strongest baseline's score on BabyAI.

arxiv:2611.23205.text: Fine-Tuning Gemma 4 Edge Models for MATLAB Signal-Processing Code with SFT and QLoRA on a Laptop iGPU. From Mehmet Altan Toksöz. Small language models can run offline on laptops, but they often mishandle conventions in digital signal processing code. This study fine-tunes Gemma edge models on checked MATLAB examples, using two adapter methods and a laptop's integrated graphics processor, then deploys the models for local use. On held-out tests, the smaller model's pass rate rose from eighteen to thirty-seven out of sixty-six, while the larger model reached forty-seven. The adapters fixed many convention errors, but rarely improved signal and noise construction, and slowed generation by seventeen to nineteen percent.

arxiv:2611.23149.text: Capability Composition in Heterogeneous Teams via Barrier-Guided Diffusion Sampling. From Diana Laura Morales and colleagues. Cooperative teams may need to perform tasks beyond any one member's abilities, but training a model usually requires costly examples of the team working together. This method instead samples team trajectories from models trained on each agent alone, while guiding the samples to obey physical constraints on how the agents can cooperate. The authors prove it can generate every trajectory that satisfies those constraints. Tests on two tasks and a multi-robot setup show that it can produce valid cooperative behavior without retraining when team members change.

arxiv:2611.23116.text: Optimal Min-Entropy Estimation with High Probability. From Qisheng Wang. Reliable min-entropy estimates help determine how unpredictable a randomness source is, including sources used in cryptographic random bit generators. This work establishes how many samples are needed to estimate min-entropy to a given accuracy with high probability, for both classical distributions and quantum states. The required sample counts scale differently: for classical data, they depend on the number of possible symbols and the desired confidence; for quantum data, they depend on the square of the dimension and the desired confidence. These bounds settle the sample complexity in both settings.

arxiv:2611.23093.text: What's in a Tree? Hierarchical n-gram models as controlled approximators of language. From Aritra Das and colleagues. Language models are hard to study in settings where context and capacity can be varied independently. Tree-grams address this with generative models that combine small groups of word relationships, while separate controls set the context window and model capacity. They outperform earlier n-gram models and remain competitive with deep transformer models. Their controlled complexity also supports more robust transfer between model sizes, and allows many routing structures to be pruned with little change in performance.

arxiv:2611.23050.text: Magflow: Differentiable Simulation of Industrial-Grade 6D Magnetic Levitation. From Philipp Hartmann and colleagues. Industrial six-degree-of-freedom magnetic levitation is hard to control because its dynamics are complex and unstable. Magflow simulates the underlying physics directly and uses the simulation to train a neural controller. The controller transfers from simulation to real hardware without further training, meets real-time demands at four kilohertz, and can levitate a mover design with no existing hand-crafted solution. This suggests that carefully matched hardware and control design are not essential for these systems.

arxiv:2611.23026.text: TPHC: Improving Hyper-Connections with Tensor-Parallel Grouped Updates. From Xinying Hu and colleagues. Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections can stabilize multiple residual streams in Transformers, but gains are limited because every stream receives the same sublayer output. TPHC uses tensor-parallel shards to create separate mixtures of streams and keep shard outputs distinct, allowing each stream to receive a different update without adding work to attention or feed-forward layers. On a one point one billion parameter model, it lowered validation loss and improved average zero-shot accuracy over the earlier method at matched stream counts. Increasing streams from four to sixteen added only nineteen percent to training time.

arxiv:2611.22998.text: Residual-Guided Lightweight Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection with a Frozen World Model. From Jiaqi Wu and colleagues. Fixed rules for choosing driving paths can miss how the right trade-off changes with the scene. This method trains a small selector to rank a fixed set of paths, while a frozen world model predicts what may happen; temporary path adjustments help guide training, but are not used at deployment. On the nuScenes validation set, it lowers average trajectory error by 3.99 percent versus the RiskWorld baseline, and by 0.83 percent versus a version trained without path adjustments. It also keeps the error lower when risk information is removed or shuffled.

arxiv:2611.22975.text: Large Language Models Have Not Yet Transformed Science. From Ron Bekkerman and colleagues. It remains unclear whether large language models have changed how science is done, because scientific practices were shifting before the models appeared. Researchers examined two and a half million full-text papers from five fields, tracking changes in language, paper structure, research ideas, and collaboration from 2015 to 2025. Most trends continued much as before 2023, apart from some word-use changes; computer science teams in Asia grew faster, while apparent declines in biomedical topic diversity mostly reflected more standardized article formats. The analysis offers a baseline for tracking future changes.

arxiv:2611.22061.text: FM-Mamba: An Efficient Native 2D Selective State Space Model with Stability-Aware Discretization. From Shengyuan Hu and colleagues. Two-dimensional Mamba models can lose image neighborhood structure when they flatten features into sequences, while direct grid-based approaches may not ensure stable updates. FM-Mamba uses a recurrence that moves along both spatial directions and adapts its step sizes to each position and direction. It derives a stability bound and projects step sizes back within it when needed, then checks stability at each position after training. A wavefront scan processes the grid directly, without flattening it.

arxiv:2611.23027.text: Right shape, wrong time: phase errors of ODE solvers in the flame problem. From Imre Boros. Stiff solvers can take far fewer steps than a standard solver on the flame model, yet still put its rising front at the wrong time. The work shows that their main error is a time shift: the computed curve has the right shape but arrives early, because small errors in early steps accumulate into a delay error. Tightening tolerances is costly. Instead, solving for the reciprocal of the model's value, which tracks time during the slow phase, cuts the error by several orders of magnitude at a similar median cost.

arxiv:2611.21927.text: Polylogarithmic Regret via Certainty Equivalence in Degenerate LQR. From Luca Vignola and colleagues. Unknown linear systems can be hard to control because learning every system parameter may require costly exploration. This work studies whether certainty equivalence can still work when control has a singular input penalty, as in minimum variance control. It proves that a short exploration phase can achieve regret that grows only with the square of the logarithm of the number of interactions, whenever the optimal controller can be identified from the data. The results also show that knowing the input matrix's range can suffice, including for underactuated systems.

arxiv:2611.22096.text: COSI: A Framework for Robustly Valid Inference. From Arun K. Kuchibhotla and colleagues. Reliable confidence sets can be hard to construct when standard statistical methods rely on assumptions that do not hold. COSI, or Confidence from Scale Invariance, splits data into batches, calculates an estimate for each, and keeps candidate values that pass a test based on how estimates change with scale. The method gives asymptotically valid confidence sets under weaker assumptions than Wald or bootstrap methods, and can achieve coverage closer to the intended level in small samples. It applies to means, regression, tensor norms, and Fréchet means.

arxiv:2611.21695.text: Stop Early, Stay Simple: Evidence Acquisition for Power System Fault and Attack Diagnosis. From S M Zia Ur Rashid and colleagues. Power system fault and attack diagnosis often checks every data source, even when a few would be enough. ActiGrid tests whether a learned policy can choose which sources to inspect and when to stop, using two public benchmarks and comparing it with simpler rules and classifiers. The learned policy adapts to the evidence, but it does not outperform simpler approaches. On the TU Delft benchmark, entropy-based stopping with a compact classifier reaches a Macro-F1 of zero point nine two eight while reading fifty-seven percent of sources; on MSU and ORNL, no method exceeds zero point four five.

arxiv:2611.21941.text: Complexity and precision in quantum associative retrieval. From Carlo A. Trugenberger. Quantum associative memories aim to retrieve stored patterns efficiently and accurately, but their advantages over classical methods are not fully clear. This work compares quantum and classical memories, where patterns are stored in a Hamiltonian, then retrieval happens through relaxation or through quantum evolution and measurement. It shows that quantum retrieval can offer an exponential complexity advantage over classical brute force search and a polynomial capacity advantage over classical neural networks when the number of patterns grows polynomially with the number of qubits.

arxiv:2611.21795.text: The Impact of Scenario Representation in Scenario-based Optimization Certification. From Stephen Crawford and colleagues. Scenario-based optimization can guarantee reliable decisions from sampled uncertainty, but its certificates may depend on how the same samples are grouped. This work studies lossless regrouping and shows that equivalent representations can reverse whether a decision is certified. It also develops a way to certify decisions directly from the original observations, without assuming nondegeneracy. In paired experiments, regrouping raised certification from three hundred eighteen to four hundred seventy-one of four hundred eighty attempts, while direct certification accepted the same number. The gains came from certificate accounting, not more information or lower decision risk.

arxiv:2611.23023.text: A singularity detecting uniformly convergent quantum wavelet framework for weakly singular nonlocal Emden, Fowler systems with quantum Mittag, Leffler sources. From Arushi and colleagues. Weakly singular solutions in nonlocal fractional systems can be difficult to compute accurately, especially near the initial time. This work develops a quantum Haar wavelet method that turns the equations into a nonlinear algebraic system, solved with a damped Newton iteration. The study proves stability and convergence estimates in a weighted norm that stays controlled despite the singularity. Tests support the estimates, and show first-order convergence even when the stated stronger regularity condition does not hold.

arxiv:2611.22711.text: Transmission Expansion and Energy Storage Planning under Great Britain's Uncertain Energy Transition Pathways. From Shengming Cao and colleagues. Planning Great Britain's power system to twenty fifty is difficult because future demand and generation are uncertain, and transmission lines and storage take different times to build. A multi-year model compares investment in transmission alone, storage alone, and both together across several energy transition pathways. Coordinated planning cuts expected unserved electricity by ninety-seven percent and total expected system cost by thirty-six percent compared with transmission-only planning. The results also show that the transition pathway strongly affects how much transmission and storage the system needs.

arxiv:2611.23174.text: Inference after coding agents. From Florian Gunsilius and colleagues. Coding agents can search through data and analyses in ways that make ordinary hypothesis tests unreliable. The work shows that, when asked to find a compelling result in data with no real effects, four leading agents report statistically significant findings between fifty-four and ninety-eight percent of the time. It proposes replaying an agent's analysis on data subsamples to measure and correct for its choices. In simulations, this brings false positive rates close to the expected five percent.

arxiv:2611.22888.text: Stopping Is Not the Limit: Understanding and Eliciting Agent Capability in Long-Horizon Vulnerability Exploitation. From Deokhyung Kang and colleagues. Vulnerability testing asks whether language model agents can turn known software flaws into working exploits, but agents often stop before using their full execution budget. On ExploitBench, researchers continued two agents beyond their first stop and found further verified gains, though the gains shrank over time. They developed a method that compresses context during repeated stops and treats claims of impossibility as unproven. With this approach, one agent reached a capability score of 67 percent at two thousand turns, showing that stopping does not always mark the limit of what an agent can do.

arxiv:2611.23196.text: Nonlinearity-preserving quantum simulation of flows in the early fault-tolerant regime. From Hansol Noh and colleagues. Ensemble prediction of nonlinear flows can be costly to run on early fault-tolerant quantum computers, because circuit costs grow with the resolution of the computational grid. This work combines compact polynomial flow models with quantum transport circuits and estimates the hardware resources needed. For a cylinder wake, the estimated preparation, simulation and sampling take one point six two hours on about five hundred and sixty thousand physical qubits to reach one percent error against a radial model. Experiments on IBM hardware also demonstrate the nonlinear transport simulation.

arxiv:2611.22019.text: Computed Permutation Trellis Coding: Near-Optimal Quantization from Two Multiplications and a 64-Byte Table. From Muhammed Fatih Balın. Low-bit quantization can waste information when it rounds each tensor value separately, while stronger joint coding often needs large tables or limits what the decoder can represent. Computed Permutation Trellis Coding uses two multiplications and a tiny table to decode values across bit widths from one to six. At four bits, it comes within 0.07 bits of the information-theoretic ideal and matches a trellis code with a table thousands of times larger. In tests on two Llama models, it also had the lowest divergence from the unquantized model among the compared methods at every tested bit width.

arxiv:2611.23021.text: Satisfiability Modulo Theories for Robust Synthesis of Signal Temporal Logic Specifications. From Philip Smith and colleagues. Robots can be given goals in Signal Temporal Logic, but finding safe plans for long deployments is difficult because current methods struggle with long time horizons and large environments. This work encodes those goals and the robots' discrete-time dynamics as constraints for Satisfiability Modulo Theories, a method for solving logical and mathematical conditions. In empirical comparisons with mixed-integer linear programming, the new approach performs best on long-horizon tasks, offering a more scalable route to planning.

arxiv:2611.22979.text: Residual-Driven Basis and Data Selection for Polynomial Approximation of High-Dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Equations. From Yuyang Huang and colleagues. High-dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations are difficult to approximate without using many polynomial terms and training samples. This work develops a greedy method that estimates how much each new basis function would reduce the equation's residual, without solving an additional adjoint problem. For data-driven models, it also selects training samples alongside basis functions by predicting how much they would reduce the fitting error. Tests on problems with up to thirty-five dimensions achieved comparable accuracy with substantially fewer terms and samples.

arxiv:2611.22176.text: Decision Stability and Model Reduction for Hamilton, Jacobi Navigation in Multiscale Flows. From Ruimeng Hu and colleagues. Autonomous vehicles may plan routes using simplified, finite-resolution models of complex flows, but accurate travel-time estimates do not always mean accurate route choices. This work studies how errors in those models affect the route a vehicle commits to. When one route is clearly best, route changes are limited and the extra travel time grows only quadratically with model error. But where two routes tie, even a tiny flow change can switch the choice, showing that model detail matters most where route decisions are fragile.

arxiv:2611.22796.text: Greedy Empirical Bayes for Density Estimation. From Taole Sha and colleagues. High-dimensional Bayesian density estimation can be accurate but costly, especially when it relies on lengthy simulation. This work introduces a method that smooths a Dirichlet process over a partition, then uses a simple bootstrap-like procedure to draw from the posterior. A greedy search builds the partition by making local split decisions, even for large datasets. The method has theoretical guarantees for adapting to real signals without splitting noise, and achieves accurate estimates and uncertainty measures at a fraction of the computational cost of competing approaches.

arxiv:2611.22855.text: CaFe: Causally Faithful Conditional Traffic Scenario Generation. From Steven Yu Tung and colleagues. Language-guided traffic simulators can make surrounding drivers react to private instructions before those instructions are visible in an instructed vehicle's behavior. To measure this intent leakage, the work introduces a paired test that holds the vehicle's path fixed while changing its instruction, and creates a large dataset of scenes with timed behavior labels. It also presents CaFe, a simulator designed to let agents respond only to what they could observe. Existing designs displaced twenty-three to eighty-three percent of nearby uninstructed agents, while CaFe eliminated measurable leakage and maintained comparable realism.

arxiv:2611.22621.text: Entanglement Lower Bounds for Symmetric Quantum Circuits. From Davi Castro-Silva and colleagues. Symmetric quantum circuits must preserve the symmetries of their input, but the role of entanglement in limiting what they can compute has been unclear. This work proves that circuits with entanglement width smaller than the number of vertices divided by the logarithm of that number cannot compute a certain graph property, even with unrestricted depth and general one- and two-qubit gates. Without that entanglement limit, symmetric circuits can compute every graph property in bounded-error quantum polynomial time. The results link entanglement limits to classical lower bounds and offer a starting point for studying quantum optimization algorithms.

arxiv:2611.22587.text: Constructions of reversible linear and DNA codes through T D,g to the n -set and (n 1,c 1 |n 2,c 2)-right polycyclic codes. From Avanish Kumar Chaturvedi and colleagues. Building reversible codes with strong parameters, including self-dual and linear complementary dual codes, is the focus of this work. It develops a construction method for reversible linear and DNA codes, and reports many maximum distance separable codes with better parameters than an earlier construction. It also gives conditions for concatenated codes to have the desired dual properties, and introduces a new class of right polycyclic codes with constructions that produce maximum distance separable codes over finite commutative rings.
